Below is a draft essay. Revise it so that it reads as if a US grade 8 student wrote it in class for a timed writing test. Keep the position it argues and keep it at about 491 words. The file must contain only the revised essay.

A measurement tool scored the draft on how it carries feeling. For each measure below it gives the current value and a target. Revise the essay so that its measures move to the targets; the tool will score the result again.
- positive charge (hedons per 1,000 words): now 89.5, target 79.5. Counts positive words such as good, love, fun.
- negative charge (dolors per 1,000 words): now 10.3, target 10.3. Counts negative words such as bad, hate, problem.
- words that carry charge (% of words): now 25.5, target 22.5. Counts share of all words that carry any feeling.
- charge under a negation (% of charge): now 8.9, target 4.4. Counts feeling words placed under not, never or n't.
- charge after an intensifier such as 'very' (% of charge): now 0.5, target 3.7. Counts feeling words placed right after very, really or so.
- charge after a contrast word such as 'but' (% of charge): now 5.9, target 0.0. Counts feeling words placed after but or however in the same sentence.
- net charge of the last fifth minus the text's mean (per 1,000 words): now 10.3, target 5.1. Counts how much more positive the last fifth is than the essay as a whole; negative means a more downbeat ending.
- how unevenly charge is spread over sentences (1 = as if words were dealt at random): now 1.1, target 1.3. Counts above 1 means the feeling is bunched into some sentences while others are plain; below 1 means it is spread evenly.

Draft:

Requiring every student to join at least one extracurricular activity is a good decision. School is supposed to prepare young people for life, and life is not only about passing tests. It also asks us to work with others, keep commitments, and find out what we care about. An activity that is required for everyone gives each student a place to learn those things.

Consider a student who arrives at high school shy and unsure of himself. He may spend every afternoon at home, avoiding the hallways and eating lunch alone. If he is asked to choose something, even something small, he might join the yearbook staff. There he meets a photographer who shows him how to frame a shot, and an editor who needs someone to write captions by Friday. Within a semester he has responsibilities, friends, and a reason to come to school. Without the requirement, he might never have taken the first step.

Critics say that forcing students into activities takes away their freedom. I understand that concern, but the requirement does not dictate which activity a student must choose. A student can pick chess club, the debate team, the robotics lab, or the school garden. The choice remains personal. What the principal removes is only the option to do nothing at all. Most adults would not describe a complete lack of involvement as freedom. It is closer to drifting.

Extracurricular activities also teach discipline that classrooms cannot always provide. A soccer player who misses practice lets down a team. A student council member who skips a meeting leaves a committee without a quorum. These obligations are real, and they are felt by peers, not just by a teacher grading a worksheet. Students learn that their effort matters to other people, and that lesson stays with them long after the season ends.

Finally, activities give students a way to discover their strengths. A grade on a math exam may show that a student can solve equations, but it rarely reveals whether she is a natural leader or a careful listener. Student council can reveal leadership. Theater can reveal confidence. Sports can reveal persistence after a painful loss. Some students will find a passion that shapes their future careers, while others will simply discover that they enjoy being part of something larger than themselves.

Some people will say that a rule like this cannot create genuine interest, and that a student who is forced into an activity will resent it. Some will, at first. But interest often grows from participation rather than coming before it. Nobody loves the piano before the first lesson. A requirement opens the door, and the student decides what to do once inside.

For these reasons, I agree with the principal. Every student deserves a chance to belong, to contribute, and to find out who they are beyond the classroom. A single required activity is a small demand that can produce large and lasting benefits.
